claim: Twenty-one participants with drug resistant epilepsy underwent a surgical procedure in which platinum recording contacts were implanted on the cortical surface as well as within the brain parenchyma.
source: Twenty-one participants with drug resistant epilepsy underwent a surgical procedure in which platinum recording contacts were implanted on the cortical surface as well as within the brain parenchyma.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section describing the participant population and surgical procedure.

claim: In six participants, one or two 96-channel microelectrode arrays (MEA; 4 × 4 mm, Cereplex I; Blackrock Microsystems, Inc, Salt Lake City, UT) were placed in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) in addition to the subdural contacts.
source: For research purposes, in six of these participants (4 female; 34.8 ± 4.7 years old) we placed one or two 96-channel microelectrode arrays (MEA; 4 × 4 mm, Cereplex I; Blackrock Microsystems, Inc, Salt Lake City, UT) in the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) in addition to the subdural contacts.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section describing the MEA implantation procedure in a subset of participants.

claim: Fast oscillations within the 80–120 Hz ripple band contribute to broadband high-frequency activity in the human cortex.
source: We demonstrate that fast oscillations within the previously identified 80–120 Hz ripple band contribute to broadband high-frequency activity in the human cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ripple oscillations exhibit a spectrum of amplitudes and durations related to the amount of underlying neuronal spiking.
source: These ripple oscillations exhibit a spectrum of amplitudes and durations related to the amount of underlying neuronal spiking.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Ripples in the macro-scale iEEG are related to the number and synchrony of ripples in the micro-scale LFP.
source: Ripples in the macro-scale iEEG are related to the number and synchrony of ripples in the micro-scale LFP, which in turn are related to the synchrony of neuronal spiking.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Micro-scale LFP ripples are related to the synchrony of neuronal spiking.
source: Ripples in the macro-scale iEEG are related to the number and synchrony of ripples in the micro-scale LFP, which in turn are related to the synchrony of neuronal spiking.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Neural activity in the human temporal lobe is organized into transient bouts of ripple oscillations that reflect underlying bursts of spiking activity.
source: Our data suggest that neural activity in the human temporal lobe is organized into transient bouts of ripple oscillations that reflect underlying bursts of spiking activity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Increases in broadband high-frequency activity are associated with overall increases in underlying neuronal spiking.
source: Arguably, the most robust link between intracranial EEG (iEEG) signals and neuronal activity has been that increases in broadband high-frequency activity are associated with overall increases in underlying neuronal spiking (Manning et al., 2009; Burke et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Successful episodic memory formation is accompanied by increases in broadband activity that progress anteriorly along the temporal cortex.
source: Successful episodic memory formation, for example, is accompanied by increases in broadband activity that progress anteriorly along the temporal cortex, which has consequently suggested that successful memory involves increases in neuronal spiking in these regions (Burke et al., 2014; Long et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ripples in the rodent medial temporal lobe are strongly associated with underlying bursts of spiking activity.
source: These ripples are strongly associated with underlying bursts of spiking activity (Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ripples have been implicated in memory formation, consolidation, and retrieval.
source: Ripples have been implicated in memory formation, consolidation, and retrieval (Buzsáki, 2015; Joo and Frank, 2018) and the bursts of spiking activity that accompany ripples are often organized into specific temporal sequences that have been hypothesized to represent the content of memory (Carr et al., 2011; Vaz et al., 2020; Pfeiffer, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fast oscillations similar to MTL ripples can be identified in the human cortex.
source: Moreover, fast oscillations that appear similar to MTL ripples can also be identified in the cortex both in animals and in humans (Khodagholy et al., 2017; Vaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical ripples observed in the human cortex are accompanied by underlying bursts of spiking.
source: Whether these cortical ripples should be considered the same as ripples in the MTL is still a matter of debate, although recent evidence has demonstrated that such cortical ripples observed in the human cortex are similarly accompanied by underlying bursts of spiking (Vaz et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ripple characteristics can vary significantly across brain areas, behavioral states, and arousal levels.
source: One of the challenges in resolving the nature of these fast oscillations that are observed in the human cortex and that appear similar to ripples observed in the MTL, however, is that ripple characteristics themselves can vary significantly across brain areas, behavioral states, and arousal levels (Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Behaviorally relevant changes in ripple characteristics have been observed in humans.
source: Ripples likely do not exist as static entities, and behaviorally relevant changes in ripple characteristics have already been observed in humans (Ngo et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ripples depend on the extent of oscillatory coupling between pyramidal neurons and interneurons.
source: Ripples depend on the extent of oscillatory coupling between pyramidal neurons and interneurons (Csicsvari et al., 1999; Stark et al., 2014), which can also change based on brain state and can differ between species and across brain regions (Klausberger et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical ripples in rodents exist on a spectrum of amplitudes that are highly correlated with underlying spiking activity.
source: Cortical ripples in rodents exist on a spectrum of amplitudes that are highly correlated with underlying spiking activity (Khodagholy et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Transient increases in high-frequency activity (70–200 Hz; HFA) were observed in individual trials immediately before participants vocalize their response during the retrieval period.
source: In an example electrode in the medial temporal lobe, we observed transient increases in high-frequency activity (70–200 Hz; HFA) in individual trials immediately before participants vocalize their response during the retrieval period (Figure 1C).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: When averaging across all trials, the increases in HFA prior to vocalization appear sustained.
source: When averaging across all trials, the increases in HFA prior to vocalization appear sustained, consistent with previous studies of episodic memory retrieval (Burke et al., 2014; Yaffe et al., 2014).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The transient increases in HFA observed in individual trials correspond to the detection of individual ripples.
source: In the same example electrode, the transient increases in HFA observed in each trial correspond to the detection of individual ripples (Figure 1C).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Both HFA and ripple rates increase prior to vocalization during successful memory retrieval trials compared to trials in which the participant failed to successfully retrieve the correct word.
source: Both HFA and ripple rates increase prior to vocalization during successful memory retrieval trials compared to trials in which the participant failed to successfully retrieve the correct word.
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: HFA increases during the one second prior to vocalization are greater during correct memory retrieval compared to incorrect memory retrieval in several anatomic regions.
source: Across participants, HFA increases during the one second prior to vocalization are greater during correct memory retrieval compared to incorrect memory retrieval in several anatomic regions (Figure 1E; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E.

claim: Ripple rates show significant increases during correct compared to incorrect trials in similar anatomic regions during the one second prior to vocalization.
source: When examining ripple rates, we also found significant increases during correct compared to incorrect trials in similar anatomic regions during this same time period (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 6B.

claim: Across ROIs from the entire cortex, the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials is positively correlated with the difference in ripple rate (r = .13, p = 6.1 × 10-4).
source: Across ROIs from the entire cortex, the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials is positively correlated with the difference in ripple rate (r = .13, p = 6.1 × 10-4; Figure 1F).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F.

claim: Within the medial temporal lobe, the positive correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the average difference in the ripple rate is r = .60, p = .00072.
source: Within two specific brain regions, the medial temporal lobe and the anterior temporal lobe, this positive correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the average difference in the ripple rate is greater (medial temporal lobe, MTL: r = .60, p = .00072; anterior temporal lobe, ATL: r = .23, p = .026; Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 6C,D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1G.

claim: Within the anterior temporal lobe, the positive correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the average difference in the ripple rate is r = .23, p = .026.
source: Within two specific brain regions, the medial temporal lobe and the anterior temporal lobe, this positive correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the average difference in the ripple rate is greater (medial temporal lobe, MTL: r = .60, p = .00072; anterior temporal lobe, ATL: r = .23, p = .026; Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 6C,D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1G.

claim: The distribution of correlations between average HFA and ripple rate across participants during baseline is significantly greater than zero (baseline r = .085 ± .018; t(20) = 4.6, p < 1 × 10-6, one-tailed t-test).
source: In both cases, the distribution of correlations across participants was consistent and significantly greater than zero (baseline r = .085 ± .018; retrieval r = .093 ± .020; t(20) = 4.6, p < 1 × 10-6, one-tailed t-test; Figure 1H).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: The distribution of correlations between average HFA and ripple rate across participants during retrieval is significantly greater than zero (retrieval r = .093 ± .020; t(20) = 4.6, p < 1 × 10-6, one-tailed t-test).
source: In both cases, the distribution of correlations across participants was consistent and significantly greater than zero (baseline r = .085 ± .018; retrieval r = .093 ± .020; t(20) = 4.6, p < 1 × 10-6, one-tailed t-test; Figure 1H).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: The relation between HFA and ripple rate was similar during memory retrieval and baseline (retrieval-baseline .0079 ± .0016, t(20) = 1.44, p = 0.083, paired t-test).
source: The relation between HFA and ripple rate was similar during memory retrieval and baseline (retrieval-baseline .0079 ± .0016, t(20) = 1.44, p = 0.083, paired t-test).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text.

claim: The relation between HFA and ripple rate was stronger during correct retrieval as compared to incorrect retrieval (correct r = .316 ± .0339, incorrect r = .259 ± .0296; t(20) = 8.7, p < 2 × 10-8; correct-incorrect .057 ± .004, t(20) = 2.40, p = .013, paired t-test).
source: However, the relation was stronger during correct retrieval as compared to incorrect retrieval (correct r = .316 ± .0339, incorrect r = .259 ± .0296; t(20) = 8.7, p < 2 × 10-8; correct-incorrect .057 ± .004, t(20) = 2.40, p = .013, paired t-test; Figure 1I).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1I.

claim: The distribution of 70–200 Hz power averaged across electrodes in each participant is significantly greater during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval (correct-incorrect: .0051 ± .0049, t(20) = 2.39, p = .013).
source: While the distribution of 70–200 Hz power averaged across electrodes in each participant is significantly greater during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval (correct-incorrect .0051 ± .0049, t(20) = 2.39, p = .013), removing the discrete 80–120 Hz ripples eliminates this difference (correct-incorrect: .0075 ± .0053, t(20) = 1.42, p = .086; Figure 1J; Figure 1—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1J.

claim: Removing the discrete 80–120 Hz ripples eliminates the difference in 70–200 Hz power between correct and incorrect memory retrieval (correct-incorrect: .0075 ± .0053, t(20) = 1.42, p = .086).
source: While the distribution of 70–200 Hz power averaged across electrodes in each participant is significantly greater during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval (correct-incorrect .0051 ± .0049, t(20) = 2.39, p = .013), removing the discrete 80–120 Hz ripples eliminates this difference (correct-incorrect: .0075 ± .0053, t(20) = 1.42, p = .086; Figure 1J; Figure 1—figure supplement 6E).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1J.

claim: HFA power during correct retrieval is significantly reduced when removing the 80–120 Hz ripples (original correct-control correct: .0096 ± .0023, t(20) = 4.21, p = 2.2 × 10-4).
source: HFA power during correct retrieval is significantly reduced when removing the 80–120 Hz ripples (original correct-control correct: .0096 ± .0023, t(20) = 4.21, p = 2.2 × 10-4).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text.

claim: After removal of the discrete ripples, the correlation across all ROIs between the participant average difference in ripple rate between correct and incorrect trials and the difference in HFA is no longer significant (r = -.042, p = .270).
source: We also examined the correlation across all ROIs between the participant average difference in ripple rate between correct and incorrect trials and the difference in HFA after removal of the discrete ripples and found that this relation is no longer significant (r = -.042, p = .270; Figure 1—figure supplement 6F,G).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 6F,G.

claim: Across ROIs from the entire cortex, there is no significant correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the difference in 120–200 Hz ripple rate.
source: Finally, to confirm that much of the 70–200 Hz power is driven by relatively band limited 80–120 Hz ripples, we repeated our analysis after detecting discrete ripple events in a higher 120–200 Hz frequency band. Across ROIs from the entire cortex, we did not find a significant correlation between the participant average difference in HFA between correct and incorrect trials and the difference in 120–200 Hz ripple rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 6H).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 6H.

claim: Ripples present in a single iEEG recording electrode overlying the MEA clearly occur simultaneously with ripples in the LFP across multiple micro-electrodes within the MEA.
source: In an example participant, ripples present in a single iEEG recording electrode overlying the MEA clearly occur simultaneously with ripples in the LFP across multiple micro-electrodes within the MEA (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Discrete ripple events are accompanied by increases in spiking activity across multiple units.
source: These discrete events are accompanied by increases in spiking activity across multiple units, and therefore transient increases in the overall population spiking rate across the MEA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: In an example participant, the average spike rate across MEA electrodes is significantly correlated with iEEG ripple band amplitude (r = .12, Pearson correlation).
source: Across all time windows in this participant, the average spike rate across MEA electrodes is significantly correlated with iEEG and LFP ripple band amplitude (spike rate v LFP amplitude r = .61, p < 1 × 10-18; spike rate v iEEG amplitude r = .12, Pearson correlation; Figure 2C).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: In an example participant, the average spike rate across MEA electrodes is significantly correlated with LFP ripple band amplitude (r = .61, p < 1 × 10-18).
source: Across all time windows in this participant, the average spike rate across MEA electrodes is significantly correlated with iEEG and LFP ripple band amplitude (spike rate v LFP amplitude r = .61, p < 1 × 10-18; spike rate v iEEG amplitude r = .12, Pearson correlation; Figure 2C).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: The relation between spiking activity and LFP ripple band amplitude is consistent and significant across participants (spike rate v LFP amplitude, Fisher z-transform: r = .751 ± .188; t(5) = 4.00, one-tailed t-test).
source: We found that the relation between spiking activity and ripple band amplitude at both spatial scales is consistent and significant across participants (spike rate v LFP amplitude, Fisher z-transform: r = .751 ± .188; t(5) = 4.00, one-tailed t-test; spike rate v iEEG amplitude: r = .118 ± .049; t(5) = 2.39, p = .031; Figure 2D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: The relation between spiking activity and iEEG ripple band amplitude is consistent and significant across participants (spike rate v iEEG amplitude: r = .118 ± .049; t(5) = 2.39, p = .031).
source: We found that the relation between spiking activity and ripple band amplitude at both spatial scales is consistent and significant across participants (spike rate v LFP amplitude, Fisher z-transform: r = .751 ± .188; t(5) = 4.00, one-tailed t-test; spike rate v iEEG amplitude: r = .118 ± .049; t(5) = 2.39, p = .031; Figure 2D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Ripples at both the macro- and micro-scale exhibit a range of amplitudes and durations.
source: We found ripples at both the macro- and micro-scale with a range of amplitudes and durations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Even when ripples have amplitudes or durations below previously used thresholds, spiking activity is present in the microelectrode recording.
source: Even when ripples have amplitudes or durations below previously used thresholds, spiking activity is present in the microelectrode recording (Figure 2—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The true relation between LFP ripple band amplitude and the spike rate is significantly greater than the shuffled distribution (true-shuffled r = .096 ± .020; t(5) = 3.312, p = .011, paired one-tailed t-test).
source: The true relation between LFP ripple band amplitude and the spike rate is significantly greater than the shuffled distribution (true-shuffled r = .096 ± .020; t(5) = 3.312, p = .011, paired one-tailed t-test; Figure 2F).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2F.

claim: The true correlations between the percentage of actively firing units and iEEG ripple amplitude across participants are significantly larger than the shuffled data (true-shuffled r = .069 ± .027; t(5) = 2.517, p = .027, paired one-tailed t-test).
source: We performed the same shuffling procedure to account for ripple duration, and found that the true correlations across participants are significantly larger than the shuffled data (true-shuffled r = .069 ± .027; t(5) = 2.517, p = .027, paired one-tailed t-test; Figure 2H).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2H.

claim: Across participants, the iEEG ripple amplitude is positively correlated with the percent of MEA electrodes exhibiting LFP ripples (% MEA electrodes with ripples, Fisher z-transform; r = .11 ± .02, p = .005).
source: In each participant, the iEEG ripple amplitude is positively correlated with the percent of MEA electrodes exhibiting LFP ripples across all detected iEEG ripples (% MEA electrodes with ripples, Fisher z-transform; r = .11 ± .02, p = .005; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: After accounting for longer durations, the true relation between iEEG ripple amplitude and the number of simultaneously detected LFP ripples is significantly greater than the shuffled distribution (true-shuffled r = .05 ± .02; t(5) = 2.543, p = .026, paired one-tailed t-test).
source: After accounting for these longer durations, we still found that the true relation between iEEG ripple amplitude and the number of simultaneously detected LFP ripples is significantly greater than the shuffled distribution (true-shuffled r = .05 ± .02; t(5) = 2.543, p = .026, paired one-tailed t-test; Figure 3B).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Across participants, the pairwise phase consistency (PPC) is significantly correlated with the maximum amplitude of the observed iEEG ripples (Fisher z-transform; r = 1.06 ± .43; t(5) = 2.34, p = .033, one-tail t-test).
source: Across participants, the PPC is significantly correlated with the maximum amplitude of the observed iEEG ripples (Fisher z-transform; r = 1.06 ± .43; t(5) = 2.34, p = .033, one-tail t-test; Figure 3E–F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The correlations between PPC and iEEG ripple amplitude across participants are significantly greater than those that would be observed by chance (true-shuffled r = .03 ± .01; t(5) = 2.28, p = .036, paired one-tail t-test).
source: In addition, the correlations across participants are significantly greater than those that would be observed by chance (true-shuffled r = .03 ± .01; t(5) = 2.28, p = .036, paired one-tail t-test; Figure 3E; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: When using only microelectrodes with detected ripples, across participants, the PPC is still significantly correlated with the maximum amplitude of the observed iEEG ripples (Fisher z-transform; r = .066 ± .02; t(5) = 3.71, p = .014, one-tail t-test).
source: We repeated this analysis using only microelectrodes with detected ripples and found that, across participants, the PPC is still significantly correlated with the maximum amplitude of the observed iEEG ripples (Fisher z-transform; r = .066 ± .02; t(5) = 3.71, p = .014, one-tail t-test).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text.

claim: Ripples are coincident above chance for all detection parameters tested.
source: We found that ripples are coincident above chance for all detection parameters tested (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This observation is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The extent to which ripples are coincident between electrodes at the two spatial scales is significantly related to the distance between them (all participants: r = -.572, p = .0035; across each participant, n = 6: r = -.595 ± .271, mean ± SEM, t(5) = -2.40, p = .0615).
source: Moreover, the extent to which ripples are coincident between electrodes at the two spatial scales is significantly related to the distance between them (all participants: r = -.572, p = .0035; across each participant, n = 6: r = -.595 ± .271, mean ± SEM, t(5) = -2.40, p = .0615; Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In all participants, spikes from all units are locked to the trough of the 80–120 Hz ripple band in the LFP signal (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all units in each participant; p = 4.8 × 10-4, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant).
source: In all participants, spikes from all units are locked to the trough of the 80–120 Hz ripple band in the LFP signal (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all units in each participant; p = 4.8 × 10-4, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant; Figure 4B).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Spiking activity is not locked to the phase of 80–120 Hz ripple band activity in the macro-scale iEEG signal (p = .12, Rayleigh test across all units and across participants).
source: We did not observe such phase consistency when examining the extent to which spiking activity is locked to the phase of 80–120 Hz ripple band activity in the macro-scale iEEG signal (p = .12, Rayleigh test across all units and across participants; Figure 4B).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4B.

claim: Spikes from all units appear locked around the trough of the 2–10 Hz low-frequency LFP signal (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test; p = 5.4 × 10-4, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant).
source: We therefore also examined the distribution of 2–10 Hz low-frequency phases present in the LFP signal around each spike and found significant locking to the trough in all participants (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test; p = 5.4 × 10-4, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant; Figure 4D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Spikes from all units appear locked around the trough of the 2–10 Hz low-frequency iEEG signal when pooled (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all units in each participant), but the apparent spike locking to the 2–10 Hz iEEG signal is not consistently at the same phase across participants (p = .70, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant).
source: Spikes from all units appear locked around the trough of the 2–10 Hz low-frequency iEEG signal when pooled, which reflects the negative deflection in the iEEG signal, but when examined separately for each participant, the apparent spike locking to the 2–10 Hz iEEG signal is not consistently at the same phase across participants (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all units in each participant; p = .70, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant; Figure 4D).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Across participants, spiking activity is significantly locked to specific high-frequency bands in the LFP (peak 86.9 Hz, p < .05, permutation test).
source: Across participants, spiking activity is significantly locked to specific high-frequency bands in the LFP (peak 86.9 Hz, p < .05, permutation test; see Materials and methods Figure 4E).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Spikes are significantly more locked to high frequencies when they arise during ripples as compared to between ripples (p < .05, permutation test).
source: Spikes are significantly more locked to high frequencies when they arise during ripples as compared to between ripples (p < .05, permutation test; Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Across participants LFP ripple amplitude exhibits a significantly stronger correlation with spike locking to the 80–120 Hz band in the true data as compared to the chance distribution (t(5) = 2.64, p = .023).
source: To account for any possible effects of ripple duration on the calculation of PPC, we compared this true distribution to a chance distribution and found that across participants LFP ripple amplitude exhibits a significantly stronger correlation with spike locking to the 80–120 Hz band in the true data as compared to the chance distribution (t(5) = 2.64, p = .023; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text.

claim: Micro-scale ripples are locked to the trough of the 2–10 Hz low-frequency band in the LFP signal in all participants (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all ripples in each participant; p = .0099, Rayleigh test across complex means, one from each participant).
source: We therefore examined the distribution of 2–10 Hz low frequency phases present in the LFP signal during each LFP ripple and found significant locking to the trough in all participants (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all ripples in each participant; p = .0099, Rayleigh test across complex means, one from each participant; Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Micro-scale ripples are locked to the 2–10 Hz low-frequency band in the iEEG signal within individual participants but at variable phases (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all ripples in each participant; p = .72, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant).
source: Micro-scale ripples are also locked to the 2–10 Hz low-frequency band in the iEEG signal within individual participants but at variable phases (p < 10-4, Rayleigh test across all ripples in each participant; p = .72, Rayleigh test across six complex means, one from each participant).
evidence: This statistical result is directly stated in the text.

claim: Many of the changes in broadband high-frequency activity captured through iEEG reflect transient 80–120 Hz oscillations.
source: Our results demonstrate that many of the changes in broadband high-frequency activity captured through iEEG reflect transient 80–120 Hz oscillations.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Short bouts of neuronal activity exist on a continuum of amplitudes and durations, and reflect underlying bursts of neuronal spiking.
source: These short bouts of neuronal activity exist on a continuum of amplitudes and durations, and reflect underlying bursts of neuronal spiking.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ripples at the micro-scale LFP signal exist on a continuum of amplitudes and durations.
source: Our data demonstrate that cortical ripples captured through human brain recordings exist on a continuum of amplitudes and durations.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2.

claim: Even ripples with smaller amplitudes or shorter durations are associated with discrete bursts of spiking activity.
source: By recording neural activity across spatial scales, we find that even ripples with smaller amplitudes or shorter durations are associated with discrete bursts of spiking activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The amplitude and duration of each ripple in the micro-scale LFP signal is related to the amount of neuronal spiking activity and the extent to which such spiking is synchronous.
source: The amplitude and duration of each ripple in the micro-scale LFP signal is related to the amount of neuronal spiking activity and the extent to which such spiking is synchronous.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 4.

claim: The amplitude and duration of each ripple in the macro-scale iEEG recording is related to the number and synchrony of ripples at the micro-scale.
source: In turn, the amplitude and duration of each ripple in the macro-scale iEEG recording is related to the number and synchrony of ripples at the micro-scale.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: The durations of ripples observed in human recordings are shorter than those observed in the rodent MTL.
source: Although the durations of ripples we observe in our human recordings are shorter than those observed in the rodent MTL, this could be related to differences in the neural architecture, and therefore differences in the latencies of activation among individual neurons, between species or between brain regions.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Fast oscillations within a narrow 80–120 Hz band of activity were identified using multiple complementary analyses.
source: Our data demonstrate similar events in the human cortex, fast oscillations within a narrow 80–120 Hz band of activity that we identify using multiple complementary analyses.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The identified events are not related to epilepsy and interictal epileptiform discharges.
source: We excluded the possibility that these events are related to epilepsy and interictal epileptiform discharges, and we find that these events are associated with ripples in the MTL.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The identified events are associated with ripples in the MTL.
source: We excluded the possibility that these events are related to epilepsy and interictal epileptiform discharges, and we find that these events are associated with ripples in the MTL.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The identified events are related to bursts of underlying spiking activity.
source: Importantly, these events are related to bursts of underlying spiking activity.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The narrow band activity (80-120 Hz) accounts for many of the changes observed in the broadband power.
source: We find that this narrow band activity accounts for many of the changes observed in the broadband power, and, of note, the cortical spiking activity in our data is locked to this narrow band.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1J and Figure 4.

claim: Cortical spiking activity is locked to the narrow 80-120 Hz band.
source: We find that this narrow band activity accounts for many of the changes observed in the broadband power, and, of note, the cortical spiking activity in our data is locked to this narrow band.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The relation between 80–120 Hz ripples and broadband high-frequency activity is not absolute and appears less robust outside of the MTL and ATL.
source: It is important to recognize, however, that this relation is not absolute and appears less robust outside of the MTL and ATL.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: The relation between 80–120 Hz ripples and broadband high-frequency activity is clearer only during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval.
source: Even within these brain regions, this relation is clearer only during correct compared to incorrect memory retrieval.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section supported by data in Figure 1I.

claim: While 80–120 Hz ripples may underlie many of the phenomena observed through broadband high-frequency activity, there are likely other neural mechanisms that contribute to the dynamics observed in the iEEG signal.
source: Hence, while 80–120 Hz ripples may underlie many of the phenomena observed through broadband high-frequency activity, there are likely other neural mechanisms that contribute to the dynamics observed in the iEEG signal.
evidence: This is a statement in the Discussion section based on inference from the data.

claim: Neural activity in the human temporal cortex is temporally organized into discrete bursts of spiking.
source: By recording spiking activity from a population of neurons in the human temporal cortex through microelectrode arrays, we find direct evidence that 80–120 Hz ripples that we observe in our data are accompanied by bursts of neuronal spiking. Hence, our data demonstrate that neural activity in the human temporal cortex may be temporally organized into discrete bursts of spiking.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The information contained within bursts of spiking activity has been recently linked with memory retrieval.
source: Our data focus on these bursts of spiking activity as participants form and retrieve memories since the information contained within these bursts has been recently linked with memory retrieval (Vaz et al., 2020; Pfeiffer, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The data cannot address whether the relation between ripples and underlying bursts of synchronized spiking is unique to just the temporal lobe or just to memory.
source: However, our data cannot address whether the relation between ripples and underlying bursts of synchronized spiking is unique to just the temporal lobe or just to memory.
evidence: This is a limitation stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Ripples have been most studied in the MTL in both animals and humans, but appear to jointly occur in brain regions that either process or receive the same information.
source: Ripples have been most studied in the MTL in both animals and humans, but appear to jointly occur in brain regions that either process or receive the same information (Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Khodagholy et al., 2017; Vaz et al., 2019; Swanson et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is possible that the relation between ripples and spiking activity is unique to brain regions that communicate directly with the MTL or that are directly involved in memory.
source: It is possible that this relation between ripples and spiking activity is unique to brain regions that communicate directly with the MTL or that are directly involved in memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The results raise the possibility that packets of spiking activity may be a general feature of neural coding in the human brain.
source: Our results, however, raise the possibility that such packets may be a general feature of neural coding in the human brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section based on inference from the data.

claim: Spiking activity within ripples appears locked to the trough of each cycle.
source: Given previous evidence demonstrating that spiking activity within ripples appears locked to the trough of each cycle, it is not surprising that we observe similar locking in our data (Le Van Quyen et al., 2008; Nitzan et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and data in Figure 4.

claim: More consistent locking of spiking activity to higher frequencies is found in the micro- compared to macro-scale.
source: We find more consistent locking of spiking activity to higher frequencies in the micro- compared to macro-scale.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claim: Synchronous spiking can occur within local neuronal ensembles while varying across ensembles.
source: This may be because synchronous spiking can occur within local neuronal ensembles while varying across ensembles.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation in the Discussion section.

claim: Spikes and ripples appear to coincide with large deflections in the iEEG and LFP trace that appear to have spectral power within a low-frequency band.
source: However, we also find that spikes, and consequently ripples themselves, appear to coincide with large deflections in the iEEG and LFP trace that appear to have spectral power within a low-frequency band.
evidence: This is an observation stated in the Discussion section and supported by data in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Locking of both spiking activity and ripples to the trough of deflections can account for phase amplitude coupling between low frequency oscillations and high-frequency activity.
source: Such locking of both spiking activity and ripples to the trough of these deflections can account for several phenomena that have been previously described in human brain recordings. For example, phase amplitude coupling between low frequency oscillations and high-frequency activity is ubiquitous in human recordings and has been linked to behavior (Canolty et al., 2006; He et al., 2010; Vaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section and supported by citations to previous literature and data in Figure 4.

claim: If many of the increases in broadband high-frequency activity are related to ripples, then phase amplitude coupling may emerge simply because ripples, and therefore spiking activity, coincide with large deflections, or sharp waves, in human brain recordings that reflect periods of concentrated synaptic inputs.
source: If many of the increases in broadband high-frequency activity are related to ripples, then phase amplitude coupling may emerge simply because ripples, and therefore spiking activity, coincide with large deflections, or sharp waves, in human brain recordings that reflect periods of concentrated synaptic inputs Buzsáki, 2015.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Some of the locking observed between low-frequency power and spiking, bursts of spiking, and therefore ripples, may also reflect locking to true low-frequency oscillations.
source: It is also possible that some of the locking we observe between low-frequency power and spiking, bursts of spiking, and therefore ripples, also reflects locking to true low-frequency oscillations.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: Low-frequency oscillations could facilitate communication between brain regions by modulating the excitability or timing of neuronal spiking.
source: If so, then this could also suggest a possible mechanism by which bursts of spiking activity may be conveyed from one brain region to another. Oscillations observed in the iEEG have been hypothesized to facilitate communication between brain regions and modulate the excitability or timing of neuronal spiking (Fries, 2015; Chapeton et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low-frequency coherence may be related to successful memory formation.
source: Indeed, low-frequency coherence may be related to successful memory formation (Shirvalkar et al., 2010; Fell et al., 2011; Lega et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two brain regions that each exhibit bursts of spiking activity can each generate high frequency ripple oscillations.
source: Our data has implications for interpreting such higher frequency coherence, as two brain regions that each exhibit bursts of spiking activity, either conveyed from one to the other directly or driven by a third region, can each generate high frequency ripple oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the Discussion section based on the data.

claim: If the underlying neuronal interactions in each brain region are similar, the ripples may appear coherent and at the same high frequency.
source: If the underlying neuronal interactions in each brain region are similar, the ripples may appear coherent and at the same high frequency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: If the underlying architecture of each region is different, then any resulting higher frequency oscillations may differ in morphology and frequency, and therefore appear desynchronized.
source: Conversely, if the underlying architecture of each region is different, then any resulting higher frequency oscillations may differ in morphology and frequency, and therefore appear desynchronized.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion section.

claim: The data argue against using fixed criteria to identify ripples.
source: Our data argue against using fixed criteria to identify these ripples, and instead demonstrate that these ripples exist on a continuum of activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Each 80–120 Hz ripple reflects bursts of neuronal spiking with varying degrees of activity.
source: As each of these 80–120 Hz ripples reflects bursts of neuronal spiking with varying degrees of activity, our data more broadly suggest these ripple oscillations may constitute one of the primary substrates of human cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion section and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ripple oscillations may constitute one of the primary substrates of human cognition.
source: As each of these 80–120 Hz ripples reflects bursts of neuronal spiking with varying degrees of activity, our data more broadly suggest these ripple oscillations may constitute one of the primary substrates of human cognition.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Data were collected at the Clinical Center at the National Institutes of Health (NIH; Bethesda, MD).
source: Data were collected at the Clinical Center at the National Institutes of Health (NIH; Bethesda, MD).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved the research protocol (11 N-0051), and informed consent was obtained from the participants and their guardians.
source: The Institutional Review Board (IRB) approved the research protocol (11 N-0051), and informed consent was obtained from the participants and their guardians.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Participants studied 93 ± 8 word pairs, and successfully recalled 30.1% ± 4.1% of words.
source: Participants studied 93 ± 8 word pairs, and successfully recalled 30.1% ± 4.1% of words.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section describing behavioral performance.

claim: A total of 1660 subdural and depth recording contacts were collected from 21 participants (79 ± 4 per participant).
source: We collected intracranial EEG (iEEG) data from a total of 1660 subdural and depth recording contacts (79 ± 4 per participant; Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The average ripple rate across electrodes across all participants was 0.35 ± 0.04 Hz.
source: We therefore identified ripples in each iEEG electrode in each participant (ripple rate .35 ± .04 Hz (mean ± SEM) across electrodes across all participants; Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 to Figure 1—figure supplement 5; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Results section.

claim: A total of 989 putative single units were identified across all sessions (average of 72 ± 21 units per participant).
source: In this manner, we identified a total of 989 putative single units across all sessions (average of 72 ± 21 units per participant).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: The average spike rate across all units was 2.82 ± .01 Hz.
source: The average spike rate across all units was 2.82 ± .01 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Across participants, after pre-processing, recordings from 78 ± 27 MEA electrodes were retained for further analysis.
source: Across the six participants, after pre-processing we retained recordings from 78 ± 27 MEA electrodes for further analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Across participants, the mean isolation score for all units was 0.93 ± 0.1.
source: Across participants, the mean isolation score for all units was .93 ± .1.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Across participants, the mean SNR for all units was 1.71 ± .12.
source: Across participants, the mean SNR for all units was 1.71 ± .12.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: IEDs overlapped with 0.79% ± 0.11% of iEEG ripples and with 1.38% ± 0.11% of LFP ripples across participants.
source: We found that IEDs overlapped with .79 ± .11% of iEEG ripples and with 1.38 ± .11% of LFP ripples across the six participants with MEAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: The mean duration of the events detected by the MODAL method was 33.5 ± 3.0 ms across participants.
source: The mean duration of the events detected by the MODAL method was 33.5 ± 3.0 ms across participants, compared to a duration of 32.8 ± 6.3 ms for the ripples that we detected using our standard approach.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the figure supplement caption for Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mean duration of ripples detected using the standard approach was 32.8 ± 6.3 ms.
source: The mean duration of the events detected by the MODAL method was 33.5 ± 3.0 ms across participants, compared to a duration of 32.8 ± 6.3 ms for the ripples that we detected using our standard approach.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the figure supplement caption for Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mean center frequency of the identified events using MODAL was 87.3 ± 3.5 Hz.
source: The mean center frequency of the identified events was 87.3 ± 3.5 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the figure supplement caption for Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Ripples are coincident across MTL and ATL regions above chance for all detection parameters tested.
source: Ripples are coincident across these regions above chance for all detection parameters tested, as indicated by a synchronization metric above one.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the figure supplement caption for Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and supported by the figure.

claim: Across participants, MEAs were implanted 14.6 ± 3.7 mm away from the closest subdural electrode with any ictal or interictal activity identified by the clinical team.
source: Across participants, MEAs were implanted 14.6 ± 3.7 mm away from the closest subdural electrode with any ictal or interictal activity identified by the clinical team.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Four out of the six participants received a surgical resection which includes the tissue where the MEAs were implanted.
source: Four out of the six participants received a surgical resection which includes the tissue where the MEAs were implanted.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the Materials and methods section.
